headline: Accutane
punch: It is not the one on your prescription.

headline: The 1982 study
body: So the famous number is that isotretinoin crushes sebum production, and the source is Goldstein 1982: seven men with severe acne, 1 mg per kg per day, for 16 weeks. | Sebum production fell **88.4%**, with a marked histological reduction in sebaceous gland size confirmed on biopsy rather than inferred. That part of the story is completely real and it has held up for forty years.

headline: Now the part nobody quotes
body: In those identical seven patients, nodulocystic lesions fell **36.2%** at the end of treatment. Not 88%. Thirty-six. | And **two of the seven got worse or did not improve at all**, despite what the paper describes as profound sebaceous gland inhibition. Their glands were shut down and their acne did not respond. That is nearly a third of the sample.

headline: The authors said it
body: Their stated conclusion: the marked sebostatic effect **may not be the sole explanation for its mechanism of action** in reducing the severity of acne. | So the single thing this drug is most famous for doing is not the whole reason it works, and that was visible in the original data in 1982. It still gets repeated as though sebum suppression is the mechanism rather than one component of it.
punch: _The sebum number is not the mechanism._

headline: Does a higher daily dose work better?
body: The assumption is that a higher daily dose produces better results, which is why people push toward 1 mg/kg and treat lower dosing as a compromise. The dose-response data does not support that. | Across 0.1, 0.5 and 1 mg/kg/day over 20 weeks, **no significant efficacy differences** were observed between them. And comparing 20 mg against 40 mg daily, the 20 mg arm worked about as well.

headline: But side effects
body: Hair loss ran at about **3.2%** below 0.5 mg/kg/day and **5.7%** at or above it. The efficacy curve flattens out and the adverse effect curve keeps climbing past the point where the benefit stopped increasing. | Those two curves flattening at different points is the entire dosing problem in one sentence, and it is why the highest tolerable dose is not automatically the right one.

headline: The big cohort
body: Lai and Barbieri 2025 followed nearly twenty thousand patients for relapse after completing a course, using insurance claims data with at least a year of follow-up afterwards. | **22.5% relapsed** and **8.2% went back for a second course of isotretinoin**. Then they asked which part of the dosing actually predicted who ended up in those groups.

headline: So which dose predicted relapse?
body: **Cumulative dosage** was associated with a decreased rate of relapse, hazard ratio 0.996 per mg/kg with tight confidence intervals of 0.995 to 0.997. More total drug, less relapse. | And **daily dose was not associated** with decreased risk of relapse or retrial. Not among patients on conventional cumulative dosage, and not among those on high cumulative dosage either.
punch: _Total dose predicted relapse. Daily dose did not._

headline: Which means the trade
body: Put those two findings together. If relapse follows the total you accumulate rather than how fast you accumulate it, then going slower costs you nothing in relapse risk. | And going slower measurably lowers your side effect rate, since side effects track the daily dose. The two findings only point one direction once you stop reading them separately.
punch: ==Slower to the same total is the same outcome.==

headline: One more thing
body: **Female sex carried a hazard ratio of 1.43** for relapse, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.35 to 1.52. A substantially higher relapse rate, entirely independent of how the drug was dosed. | Which is worth knowing before anyone treats a relapse as evidence that their dosing was wrong. Some of the variance in who relapses is not a dosing variable at all.
punch: Not every relapse is a dosing problem.

headline: A practical absorption note
body: Isotretinoin is lipophilic, and its absorption roughly **doubles** when taken with around 20 grams of fat compared with taking it on an empty stomach. | So the dose you swallow and the dose that actually enters you are different numbers, and that difference is larger than most of the dosing arguments people have. How you take it moves the real dose more than adjusting the prescription does.
punch: How you take it changes the dose.

headline: What holds up overall
body: Sebum suppression is real at around 88% and is not the full mechanism, by the original authors' own conclusion. Daily dose plateaus for efficacy while side effects keep climbing past that plateau. | And relapse tracks the cumulative total rather than the daily number, measured in nearly twenty thousand people. Count the total, not the daily.
